To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the embryonic brain is hypersensitive to ionizing radiation, with the VZ/SVs and IZ being distinct in their sensitivity to DNA DSBs.

(i) the VZ/SvZ is hypersensitive in response to low levels of DNA double-stranded break formation; (ii) the VZ is highly proliferative and has a functional G2M checkpoint; and (iii) the IZ is hypersensitive, in response to persisting double-stranded breaks.
the VZ/SvZ is sensitive to acute DSB induction and the IZ is sensitive to persisting DSB induction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of DNA repair and apoptosis in embryonic brain development.
the role of the DNA double strand break (DSB) repair protein DNA ligase IV in the developing and mature brain.
understanding the molecular mechanisms that underpin the sensitivity of the embryonic brain to radiation-induced apoptosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the VZ/SvZ is hypersensitive and the IZ is hyporesponsive to radiation.
the embryonic brain, in contrast to adult, is sensitive to DNA damage, but this sensitivity depends on the cell compartment.
DNA Ligase IV is a critical factor in the maintenance of normal brain development and function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the VZ/SvZ and IZ are both hypersensitive to DNA damage, but the underlying mechanism of sensitivity differs.
the IZ and VZ/SVz regions of the developing brain have distinct sensitivities to DNA damage, which are dependent upon both the number of DSBs and the duration of DSB persistence.
the VZ/SvZ is sensitive to low numbers of radiation-induced DNA DSBs, while the IZ is sensitive to high numbers of DNA DSBs and that the VZ is sensitive to endogenous DNA DSBs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple mechanisms that can cause microcephaly, and that these mechanisms may be distinct in different regions of the brain.
DNA repair is critical for normal brain development and function.
DNA damage response pathways are differentially regulated in the VZ, SVZ, and IZ, and this is critical in the maintenance of brain homeostasis.
